query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the particle delivery via spray distance adjustment – specifically shifting to a 300–350 mm nozzle standoff distance on the HVAF‐i7 torch – will increase particle velocity and kinetic energy so that the FeCoNiCrAl powder builds up a thicker, well‐adherent bond coat while still keeping as-sprayed oxidation minimal.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with 15–45 μm feedstock used in previous HVAF processes
generation.intervention: Modify the HVAF-i7 process by setting the spray (nozzle-to-substrate) distance to 300–350 mm rather than using the default for this torch
generation.conditions: Deposition performed on bond-coat substrates (including challenging geometries such as internal diameters as low as 120 mm) under otherwise standard HVAF-i7 settings and elevated-temperature service conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Increased particle velocity enhances the in-flight kinetic energy, improving the momentum transfer at impact. This produces more completely melted or thoroughly deformed splats that bond better and build up a thicker layer while shortening particle residence time in oxygen-rich environments to limit oxidation.
generation.mechanism: By positioning the substrate at an optimal spray distance (300–350 mm), the particles enter the substrate with higher velocity – as seen in analogous MCrAlY studies – which increases deposition efficiency. The enhanced impact energy promotes denser and thicker splat formation without additional oxidation because the reduced flight time limits exposure to ambient oxygen.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significantly thicker, well-bonded, and minimally oxidized bond coat will be produced compared with the baseline HVAF-i7 process using the same feedstock, and this effect should persist even when applied to internal diameters as small as 120 mm.
generation.baseline: The current HVAF-i7 depositions using 15–45 μm powder which yield acceptable quality but insufficient coating thickness
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under standard HVAF-i7 settings and for the FeCoNiCrAl alloy composition; however, if other parameters (e.g. powder flow rate or torch power) are significantly altered, the outcome may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis builds on the observation from conventional MCrAlY bond coat studies that higher particle velocity (achieved at optimized spray distances of 300–350 mm) modestly increases deposition efficiency (evidence combined from the query prompt and PMC10820071::web::010). Extending this effect to the HVAF-i7 process with FeCoNiCrAl alloys is plausible yet remains unproven, warranting experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of bond coat depositions using the HVAF-i7 torch on identical substrates (including specimens with internal diameters of 120 mm) while varying only the nozzle standoff distance (e.g., 250 mm, 300 mm, 350 mm, and 400 mm). All other deposition parameters (feedstock, gas flows, torch power) are held constant.
measurements: Oxidation level via XRD/EDS analysis of as-sprayed coatings
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized spray distance (300–350 mm) does not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness and deposition efficiency—without incurring higher levels of as-sprayed oxidation or degradation in adhesion—compared to the baseline condition, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC.
